name: Immune Power diet

card.summary: A 1985 diet-book program that removes seven common foods in the belief that strengthening immunity improves health, weight and, in followers' terms, overall vitality and appearance.
card.note: Nutrition reviewers have raised concerns about nutrient adequacy and high-dose vitamin B6.

quick.overview:
The Immune Power Diet comes from physician Stuart Berger's 1985 book. It holds that hidden food sensitivities weaken immunity, and that cutting out foods such as dairy, wheat, eggs and sugar, then reintroducing them, restores health and helps with weight.

In appearance terms, the claimed payoff is weight loss and clearer, healthier-looking skin and energy from a cleaner diet. Reviews by dietitians and medical commentators in the 1980s were critical of its premises, and no controlled trials of the program are known.
quick.how: The program has an elimination phase avoiding what Berger called the Sinister Seven (dairy, wheat, yeast, eggs, corn, soy and sugar), followed by gradual reintroduction of foods, plus supplements. Followers use it as a weight-loss and detox plan.
quick.risks: A 1987 dietitian review judged several popular diets including this one to give misleading information or unbalanced, low nutrient intakes. Critics noted that large vitamin B6 amounts can cause nerve damage. Anyone with a real food allergy or medical condition would normally consult a clinician.

lead: The Immune Power Diet is a diet program described in Dr. Berger's Immune Power Diet, published in 1985 by physician Stuart M. Berger (1953-1994). It claims that many people have hidden food allergies that burden the immune system, and that eliminating certain foods, detoxifying and supplementing restores immune function [1].

People are drawn to it for weight loss and general vitality; the book linked an "immune hypersensitivity response" to conditions ranging from obesity to AIDS [1]. For appearance, the relevant chain is slimmer body weight and the belief that eliminating foods improves skin and energy.

A 1987 overview of fad diets by a research dietitian listed it among diet books viewed as providing misleading information or unbalanced, low nutrient intakes [2]. Nutritionists and the Harvard Medical School Health Letter also criticised it [1].

chain: Eliminate seven common foods and take supplements
Lower calorie intake and belief in reduced inflammation
Claimed weight loss and healthier-looking skin
angle.text: Followers use the elimination plan as a structured weight-loss approach. Benefits to skin and vitality are claims made in the book rather than findings from controlled trials.

infobox: Dairy, wheat, yeast, eggs, corn, soy, sugar

paras: The book's central claim is that undiagnosed food hypersensitivity affects a large share of people and harms immune function. Readers avoid seven foods, which Berger called the Sinister Seven, and can gradually reintroduce them, no more than once every four days [1]. The program also recommends detoxification and dietary supplements, including megadoses of vitamin B6 [1].

Nutritionists called the diet unscientific. The Harvard Medical School Health Letter described the book as fiction built on mistaken ideas about food allergies [1]. Berger's claim that 30 percent of Americans have food allergies was disputed; a 2017 study put the figure below 4 percent [1]. Nutritionist Jack Z. Yetiv noted that large B6 doses can be toxic and cause irreversible nerve damage [1]. Immunologists do not list the diet as an effective AIDS treatment [1].
The 1987 review by a research dietitian grouped it with other fad diets of the time [2][3].

timeline.event: Dr. Berger's Immune Power Diet published [1].
Nutrition & the M.D. overview of popular and fad diets discusses the program [2].
Berger dies; autopsy attributes death to hypertension and cardiovascular disease [1].
